name: temporal-object
intent: Give a long-lived domain object one stable identity and represent each change as an immutable, effective-dated version of the whole object, so clients can ask for it as it is now or as it was at any date without versioning every attribute separately.
problem: Most attributes of the object change over time and the business talks about those changes as versions - contract amendments, policy endorsements, price revisions, org-chart changes. Callers need 'the contract as of 1 March' while other objects must keep referring to the same contract after it changes. Versioning each attribute independently spreads history across every accessor, lets a read recombine field values that were never true at one moment, and leaves nothing to name when the business wants to discuss a specific amendment.
context: Long-lived business entities whose value lies in their history as a whole: contracts and their amendments, insurance policies and endorsements, price lists and product terms, payroll and personnel records, regulatory or clinical revisions, and version-control-like artifacts where the filename is the continuity and each committed revision a version. It applies when history is part of the domain - queried, referenced, amended retroactively - and not merely an audit trail, and it survives persistence unchanged: the relational form is a versions table keyed by identity plus effective date, with no row for the continuity itself.
benefits: Stable identity: other objects hold one reference to the continuity for the object's whole life and never rebind it when a version is appended.
Whole-object consistency: each version is a complete, internally consistent state, so a read can never mix old terms with a new fee the way independent per-property histories can.
Business vocabulary: amendments, endorsements and revisions become first-class objects that people can name, cite in documents and diff.
One temporal entry point: historic reads are 'object at date' instead of a date threaded through every getter, and the current value is just the default as-of read.
History integrity: immutable published versions keep past states reconstructible for reconciliation, dispute and audit, and a current-state bug cannot silently rewrite the past.
Retroactive and scheduled changes are ordinary model operations: a version with a past or future effective date is inserted, not special-cased.
tradeoffs: Storage grows with change frequency x object size: whole-object snapshots duplicate every unchanged field, and delta storage trades the space back for reconstruction cost.
Every read pays indirection through the continuity and every write pays a copy plus an insert - negligible for a configuration object, visible for hot, frequently-updated entities.
Immutability is a discipline, not a guarantee: shallow copies of records, Data values or frozen objects still share nested collections, so a published version can be rewritten by accident.
Retroactive edits force the effective-time vs record-time decision: once 'as of' can mean 'as we knew it then', the model needs a second time axis or an explicit audit log beside the versions.
As-of reads of reference-valued fields drag in the object graph: a version pointing at 'the current customer' mixes times, so references must be versioned too or documented as resolved by reference.
Queries and indexes get harder: persisted forms need (identity, effective_date) keys, as-of joins and period predicates instead of plain current-state selects.
Keeping every version collides with retention and erasure rules, and the current version becomes a hot row - both need explicit policy (pruning, archiving, materialized current state).

participants.responsibility: The object people refer to throughout its changes: carries the stable identity and the few truly immutable attributes, owns the version history, answers current reads from the newest version and historic reads through as-of.
An immutable snapshot of the changeable state, valid from its effective date until the next version's date; the object the business names when it says 'the 1998 amendment'.
The date (or period) from which a version is in force - the Effectivity that orders the history and defines the boundary semantics of as-of lookups.
The ordered collection of versions keyed by effective date, with floor lookup for as-of reads and an insertion point for retroactive or scheduled amendments.
The copy-on-write step of the update path: copy the version in force, change the copy, publish it at its effective date - never edit a published version.
Reads current state through the continuity's default accessors, reads history through as-of, and asks for a working copy when it needs to change the object.
Optional stand-ins returned when the requested date precedes the first version or follows the end of the history, so clients never branch on null.

use_cases: Insurance policies and endorsements: premium, coverage and beneficiary as of the date of a claim or a reinstatement.
Contracts amended by dated documents (credit cards, telecoms, procurement): each amendment is a version the business can name and send.
Price lists and product terms: an order must be priced with the terms in force on the order date, not with today's list.
Payroll and personnel records: pay rates and position assignments revised retroactively after late notification, with recomputation of affected periods.
Regulatory, clinical and legal records where every correction is a new version and the history itself must be auditable and reconstructible.
Version-control-like artifacts: a stable file or artifact identity with committed revisions (source control: filename as continuity, revisions as versions).

SQL Server system-versioned (temporal) tables: the current table is the continuity, the paired history table holds whole-row versions bounded by ValidFrom/ValidTo period columns, and FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF is a built-in as-of operation over both.

Datomic: entity idents persist for the life of the entity while datoms accrete immutably, and as-of/since database filters give valid-time and transaction-time views - the two time axes the effective-vs-recorded-time decision needs.

django-simple-history: adding HistoricalRecords to an ordinary Django model yields an immutable whole-row snapshot per save and an as_of(date) query on the instance - history on self bolted onto plain entities, with HistoricForeignKey resolving relations at the same historic point.
avoid_when: Only a few properties are temporal - use Temporal Property (date-indexed accessors) or Effectivity (a validity Range attached to the fact) instead of versioning whole objects.
History is needed only for audit or forensics and never read by the domain - an audit log or change-data-capture beside a plain mutable entity is simpler.
The domain needs the sequence of events and their causes rather than the states between them - model domain events (event sourcing) and treat versions as projections.
Updates are so frequent and the objects so large that whole-object snapshots explode storage (counters, telemetry, balances) - keep a mutable current row plus periodic snapshots.

Each revision is genuinely a different thing rather than a version of the same thing (separate purchase orders, distinct invoices) - model separate entities and stop pretending they share an identity.
The current state is all anyone ever reads and changes replace it wholesale - a plain entity with updated_at and a version number for optimistic locking is enough.
anti_patterns: Mutating a published version in place, so the history records what the code did rather than what was in force.
Versioning every attribute independently 'just in case': per-property histories recombine into states that never existed and leave nothing for the business to name.
Creating a fresh continuity object on every change, forcing every other object to rebind its reference and destroying the identity the pattern exists to protect.
Keeping only the latest effective date (overwriting it on amendment), which makes the version list unnavigable and as-of queries guesswork.
Adopting a version store without an as-of API and hand-rolling date predicates in every caller, so boundary rules drift apart across the codebase.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: identity and behaviour live in the continuity, state in the version.
Information hiding: ordering, boundary semantics and storage stay behind a single as-of operation.
Immutability of published state: a version is a value, and change is a new value.
Stable identity: the entity keeps its identity across changes while its state changes value - the same split as entity vs value object.
Do not repeat yourself: one lookup and one boundary rule for all historic reads.
best_practices: Name the two roles in the ubiquitous language (Contract / ContractVersion, Policy / Endorsement) so the model speaks the way the business does.
Publish by copy-on-write: take a working copy of the version in force, change the copy, insert it at its effective date; never edit a published version.
Give every version an effective date - and, where retroactive edits are possible, a separate recorded date - with half-open validity ranges and one documented comparison rule.
Keep the history ordered and indexed by effective date and expose as-of through one method; callers must never sort, scan or compare versions themselves.
Return a special case (Missing/Invalid Version or an explicit absent result) instead of null when the date falls outside the history.
Decide and document how references inside a version resolve - as of the same date, or explicitly 'current by reference'.
Apply a retention policy to old versions and keep as-of queries off the hot path (materialize or cache the current version, archive the rest).
sources: Martin Fowler, Temporal Object, Further Enterprise Application Architecture development (eaaDev draft, 2004) - continuity and version roles, explicit class vs amendment-chain forms, the versions-table form, and the contrast with Temporal Property.
Martin Fowler, Temporal Patterns (eaaDev narrative) - Snapshot, Temporal Object, Effectivity, and the two dimensions of time (actual vs record).
Anderson, History on Self, PLoP'98 submission (PLoPD 4) - the same pattern under Anderson's name, cited by Fowler as such.
Arnoldi, Beck, Bieri & Lange, Time Travel: A Pattern Language for Values That Change (EuroPLoP 1999) - Version History, Perspective, Effective Date, Missing Version, Invalid Version.

SQL Server system-versioned (temporal) tables - the pattern shipped in an engine: current table plus history table, ValidFrom/ValidTo period columns, and FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF/FROM...TO/BETWEEN/CONTAINED IN as-of queries.
Datomic History and time-travel filters - bitemporal as-of (valid-time) and transaction-time reads over an immutable accreting store with stable entity identities.
django-simple-history querying docs - HistoricalRecords snapshots per save, instance.as_of(datetime) point-in-time reads, and HistoricForeignKey for time-consistent relations.

Temporal table considerations and limitations - the misuse case: system-versioned history is record-time only, begins at enablement and cannot be edited retroactively, so it is not a complete as-was-known audit on its own.
